You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: G5613

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "As, like (comparative); when, while (temporal); about (approximative); how! (exclamatory); as if; so as to; since"
  Readable gloss: "The Greek particle hos is one of the New Testament's most hardworking function words, appearing over 500 times with a semantic range strikingly parallel to its Hebrew counterpart ka'asher. At its core it draws comparisons — 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matt 5:48) — but it flexes readily into temporal, approximative, exclamatory, and even purposive territory. Its flexibility is mirrored across languages: French comme covers comparison and time, Spanish como spans comparison and exclamation, while German wie handles comparison, time, and exclamation alike. The particle's ability to hover between these functions is part of what makes Koine Greek so compact and expressive."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "comparative: as, like"
    Enriched: Comparative: 'as,' 'like' — the dominant sense at roughly 78% of occurrences, drawing a likeness or manner parallel. 'Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven' (Matt 6:10) and 'be perfect as your Father is perfect' (Matt 5:48) are paradigmatic. Spanish como, French comme, and German wie all converge here with their default comparative meaning.
    Existing Spanish translations: como
  Sense 2: "temporal: when, while"
    Enriched: Temporal: 'when,' 'while' — introducing a time clause, especially in Luke-Acts narrative. 'When the days of his service were completed' (Luke 1:23) and 'when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting' (Luke 1:41). Korean ttae ('when') and Spanish cuando distinguish this sharply from the comparative como, confirming a genuine temporal sense.
    Existing Spanish translations: como, cuando
  Sense 3: "approximative: about"
    Enriched: Approximative: 'about,' 'roughly' — used with numbers or quantities to express estimation. 'About two thousand' swine (Mark 5:13), 'about four thousand' men (Mark 8:9), and 'about twelve years old' (Luke 8:42). Spanish como retains ambiguity, but Korean yak and Hindi lagbhag unambiguously signal approximation.
    Existing Spanish translations: como
  Sense 4: "exclamatory: how!"
    Enriched: Exclamatory: 'how!' — introducing an exclamation of degree or manner. 'How the women who had come with him from Galilee observed the tomb' (Luke 23:55) and 'how she had been healed immediately' (Luke 8:47). Spanish cuan/como and German wie serve double duty as exclamatory particles, confirming this reading across traditions.
    Existing Spanish translations: como, cuán, cómo
  Sense 5: "hypothetical comparison: as if"
    Enriched: Hypothetical comparison: 'as if,' 'as though' — introducing an imagined or counterfactual scenario. Peter disclaims credit 'as if by our own power we had made him walk' (Acts 3:12), and plotters feign intention 'as though they would inquire more closely' (Acts 23:15). French comme si and Korean machi help distinguish this from factual comparison.
    Existing Spanish translations: como
  Sense 6: "purpose: so as to"
    Enriched: Purpose: 'so as to,' 'in order to' — expressing intended result, typically with an infinitive. Jesus sent messengers ahead 'so as to prepare for him' (Luke 9:52), and Paul counts his life of no value 'so as to finish my course' (Acts 20:24). Spanish para and French pour confirm the purposive reading distinct from comparison.
    Existing Spanish translations: para
  Sense 7: "temporal: since"
    Enriched: Temporal starting-point: 'since,' 'from the time that' — marking a temporal origin. Only one occurrence: 'How long since this has been happening to him?' (Mark 9:21). Spanish desde que and French depuis que distinguish this backward-looking temporal sense from the simultaneous 'when' of sense 2.
    Existing Spanish translations: desde-que
